   PLEASE SEND YOUR TEXTFILE!
Text is accepted in any form for
OUTLETTERS: wordprocessor files
(say which),typed or handwritten
letters. However, PLEASE send us
a textfile if possible so your
letter needn't be typed again!
The easiest for us to edit are
Tasword 2 files with the right
margin set at 32 but a textfile
in ANY format is appreciated!

Please state if there should be
parts of your letter you do not
wish published but we always use
our discretion anyway. Letters
may also be edited for clarity
and length... Please ask if you
welcome direct correspondence
from other OUTLET readers and we
will publish your full address.

From M.C. Baldridge, GWENT

I am writing to see if you could
help me with a problem I have in
printing from OUTLET [via +3].

When I bring them up on screen
there is an instruction on the
bottom of the screen asking if I
want to print out the PAGE or
ALL. When I type "P" or "A" I
get a sub-menu for the printer.
I have a Citizen 120D printer
configured for Epson but cannot
print out. I set the Baud rate
at 9600 and press ENTER but
still nothing happens.

Could you please advise me if I
am doing anything wrong or if I
should be doing something else.

Brian Cavers to M.C. Baldridge

The fact that you are trying to
set the baud rate tells me you
are using the RS232 port of the
+3 rather than the Centronics
port which is the default and
more normal printer port.

The option to change the baud
rate was included in OUTLET for
Interface 1 users and recently
removed now that we no longer
produce a microdrive version. If
you look at the +3 option you
will see it says "CENTRONIC". I
must admit it never occurred to
me that the baud rate option
might have been taken as for the
+3 because very few people use
the RS232 for printing.


Anyway, one way round it is for
you to initialize your +3 to use
the RS232 port before loading
OUTLET. If you look at page 171
of your +3 manual you will see
you need to enter...

       FORMAT LPRINT "R"

This only needs doing once in a
session unless you reset or
switch off - it does not need
doing every time you print any-
thing.

You can enter it in three ways..


1. Enter +3 BASIC and enter it
   as a direct command followed
   by ENTER and then load OUTLET


2. Enter a small program...

   10 FORMAT LPRINT "R"
   20 CLS
   30 PRINT AT 10,5;"PUT OUTLET
      IN DRIVE. PRESS A KEY"
   40 PAUSE 0
   50 LOAD "DISK"
                 ...then save it
   on another disc with...

   SAVE "DISK" LINE 10
                ...then load it
   first before loading OUTLET.

3. Enter the FORMAT LPRINT "R"
   in OUTLET itself and resave.
   (a)RESET. (b)MERGE "CONTENTS"
   (c) LIST 1420. (d) ADD it to
   the line. (e) RUN 9980 to
   resave.


I have made a note that when the
Opus version of OUTLET finishes
in September I will see if I can
add an option to the submenu to
offer RS232 on the +3.Meanwhile,
please write again if you have
any trouble with any of the
above.
                          Brian

From Brian Gaff, SURREY

Dear Brian,

Regarding your plans for a PC
OUTLET, as you are probably
aware, I handle registrations
for the Spectrum Emulator for
the PC. Now that this has
Microdrive emulation, and over
100 registered users, it struck
me that it might be an idea to
bring back the Microdrive
version of Outlet.

My idea would be to put it out
as MDR files. These are Micro-
drives held as files on the PC's
disc. A 720K floppy could hold
around five, each holding over
100K, so it would be no worse
than a +3, space-wise.

You would not need FAILSAFE, as
a BATCH file and .Z80 starting
file would make sure the carts
were loaded. Of course, if you
opted for a HD disc, you could
always include some pure PC
software, though it could not be
linked.

I have the mailing list of users
and it stuck me that if you did
decide to do this, we could also
involve FORMAT, and split the
mailout costs three ways.I would
sell tape interfaces, FORMAT
could shift some mags, and you
Z80 versions of Outlet. Anyway,
what do you and the users think?
I have no idea what the take up
rate would be, but then what is
predictable these days?


Now YS is being killed off, I
think we need some kind of adv-
ertising strategy too.I am going
to contact YS and see if a dir-
ectory of Spectrum contacts can
be published.I advise we ALL do!

With the death of the mag, games
sources will be required, and I
think its time we approached the
software houses about the poss-
ibility of A) them advertising
with subscription mags and B)
getting them to release old pro-
duct to us either as PD-unlikely
- or on a low royalty basis for
distribution on disc. Of course,
I include more serious software
in this too, its just that there
are bound to be gamers out there
stuck for a source of info or
product.                 - Brian

Brian Cavers to Brian Gaff

When I come to do this month's
conversions I'll have a look at
what would be involved - how
much time it might need etc. It
should not be so difficult as
producing the real microdrive
version in theory because I
would not need to transfer it
physically via tape microdrive
with all the resulting hassle of
testing on cartridges which were
so very unreliable. However, we
all know how things which look
simple turn out to be very time-
consuming. It all depends I
suppose on what sort of reaction
we get from readers etc. I don't
want to finish up doing a half-
day's work for only a dozen
sales!

We used to have a VERY poor
response to our adverts in YS so
I doubt their readers are really
the type to like OUTLET. Still,
we'll think it over.

I suppose I sound a bit negative
but that's what comes of six
years of hard, grinding labour
trying to meet every minority's
needs with nothing to show for
it! Our main hope lies with the
full PC magazine I think.

                     - Brian

Dear Brian and Ron,

    SPECTRUM EMULATOR FOR PC

I must say that Gerton Lunter
has again excelled with the
latest version of his Spectrum
Emulator for IBM PC compatible
computers. This is a fantastic
program which now fully emulates
either 48K or 128K Spectrums,
including tape input (hardware
diagram included) and software
emulation of Interface 1/
Disciple /+D with UP TO EIGHT
Microdrives /floppy disk drives.


This means that although the PC
in Emulator mode is restricted
to the usual 48K Spectrum's
memory (with extra "sideways"
memory in 128K mode for ramdisk,
etc. use) the PC's hard disk can
now be used just as if the
"Spectrum" had the 8 drives
attached with their resultant
storage capacities available,
including "formatting" the
Microdrive cartridges/disk,
"inserting" and "removing" them.

If these were not enough, Gerton
has even included a software
emulator for his hardware
"Samram" (nothing to do with a
Sam computer) which gives an
additional 32K of "sideways"
memory.


I find that the 48K emulator
works at a FASTER speed than the
Spectrum on a 386 PC, although
the speed can be reduced if
required for games, etc. However
some older PCs, may run more
slowly than the Spectrum.


The 128K emulator is currently a
little disappointing as it is
slower than the Spectrum when
ENTERing programs and commands,
but I hope that the running of
128K programs will not suffer. I
am unable to confirm this as I
have yet to write any 128K
programs with the emulator or to
receive a copy of the 128K
Disciple/+D converter.


Although the emulator will
switch between 48K and 128K I
find that programs "snapped" and
converted from 48K mode are lost
on switching to 128K.

Whilst these few comments cannot
fully do justice to the
capabilities of the emulator I
recommend it as a thoroughly
good buy for Spectrum owners
with access to PCs, or for PC
owners wishing to use Spectrum
program/skills.

Full on-disk documentation is
included which prints out to 64
pages of A4. However, the basic
operation of the emulator is
simple.


Available for `15 registered or
limited facility shareware for
`3.50 from...

 BG SERVICES, 64 Roebuck Road,
  Chessington, Surrey, KT9 1JX
          081-397-0763

                    ...or can be
included with other programs,
all supplied converted for PC,
from...

       FLEXIBASE SOFTWARE
       20 The Parklands,
   Droitwich, Worcs. WR9 7DG.



                  David Wornham

From Malcom Perry,KIDDERMINSTER

I recently acquired a second
hand drive on the basis of
"untested" which quite often
translates to "does not work".
Whether repairable is another
matter!! This was one of the
later dual DD/HD type. The drive
exhibited all the symptoms of
track alignment and track 0
sensor being incorrect.

Having adjusted drives before,it
was approached with confidence -
only to be shot down when it was
found the"adjustments" consisted
of sliding in slots then solidly
glued in position on both the
stepper motor and T0 adjuster
with not a screw in sight!


I had to resort to devious
tactics with a stanley knife and
scientifically-applied brute
force to break the bonds.

I presume this method is found
to be quicker and cheaper at
manufacture than having to use
such high-tech tools like a
screwdriver. It does though show
little consideration for future
service but there again it seems
these days you are not supposed
to repair things. As I was told
not so long ago "...No we cannot
let you have a `30 replacement
part for one item or repair the
other `100 one just over 12
months old. We will be happy to
sell you other `200 and `100
replacements". Needless to say I
did not take up the offers.

I am now in a quandary. How long
do I leave it before adding more
glue to be certain the adjust-
ment is OK but if not glued then
likely to move from use? How
much simpler screws are!!!

Like you, I pondered how such a
random set of numbers could
program a video recorder.

[using the VideoPlus timer - BC]

The only thing that seemed to be
slightly consistent was that the
smallest number seemed to occur
about 6.30pm but it was not
consistent on which channel the
lowest number was - so perhaps
that is a red herring.


I gave up how a number like 27
could provide all the inform-
ation in one case but in others
it needs a string of 8 numbers.
There again, was a 2-digit
number an error in printing as I
have also seen a mix of numbers
and letters at odd times?

However, considering the handset
is no doubt processor-controlled
and the numbers computer-gener-
ated (I somehow cannot see the
editor counting it out on his
fingers)the codes do not need to
have any humanely-logical form
but just be pure data. Take Z80
data. In most cases it means
nothing on its own without the
surrounding program code.


The largest string of numbers
seems to be 8. Could it be that
perhaps all numbers are 8 digits
with leading zeros suppressed?
There do not seem to be trailing
zeros as you get,such as 234500.
The device does not have to use
numbers left to right but could
be right to left or in groups in
either direction.

I still have no idea how the
thing works and numbers relate
but it does look more like a
random selection picked out of a
hat.

Relating to the UniDOS command
codes item, there is some
additional information that may
be of interest...


On trying the C.C. in its simpl-
est form i.e., call from and
return to BASIC, I was finding
the computer crashed. This only
occurred with a 128K. There was
no problem with a 48K machine.
With thanks to Steve Warr it
turns out for some unexplained
reason the 128 treats the HL'
(alternative HL pair) registers
differently to a 48K and after
the Unidos C.C. has been
completed this register is not
being correctly set to enable a
correct return to BASIC.

The solution is to set HL' to
#2758 (hex) after the C.C. and
before returning to BASIC. If
the C.C. is incorporated in a
larger MC routine and returning
to MC, things should be O.K.

Again, another thanks to Steve
for a solution to my problem
that using the Disciple on
UniDOS.I was not getting correct
loading and running of an
AUTOload file on BOOT. Seems
this was due to a FLAG not being
correctly set and the stack
becoming corrupted. This is
corrected by doing the following
POKES and resaving the BOOT
file...
        POKE @6618,53025
        POKE @6620,13882
        POKE @6622,49920
        POKE @6624,(PEEK @452)
        POKE @6625,(PEEK @453)
        POKE @452 ,14810

This does seem to have made the
autoload and run more reliable.


Finally, it may be of interest
the system can be rebooted if
needed without having to switch
off - by POKE @7667,0 then RUN.

It is a refreshing change to
have received such back up to
the UNIDOS from Steve Warr in
helping with the problems and
spending time in offering
possibilities and test routines
to establish problem areas
almost by return of post -
especially as two approaches to
S.D Software, who sell the
Unidos, asking about the command
codes, have remained unanswered
and it took some 6 weeks and a
reminder to supply the Unidos
create file manual with no
explanation or apology.
                  Malcolm Perry

From Ron Cavers

      THE VIDEO+ MYSTERY
     (A Possible Solution)
The Video+ puzzle (how to encode
a television program start date
& time, it's length & channel No
- all within an 8 digit No.)
gave me a few restless nights
until I came up with a solution.
I don't think for one minute
that it is the correct answer
but it seems to work and that is
enough to let me sleep nights.

I thought the answer might be
found by converting any numbers
into their binary equivalents,
compressing them in some way,
and then encoding them (or vice
versa) just to fool the puzzle
addicts.

It also seemed to me that some
kind of look-up table was
necessary in order to reduce the
numbers involved & Brian's
suggestion that the times of
programs (or lengths) could be
in 5 minute blocks was a good
starting point. If,for instance,
an hour is listed as 0, 5, 10,
15, 20 etc, then any part of the
list can be stored as a number
0 to 11 (instead of 0 to 59).

The saving is more obvious if
the highest numbers are
converted to binary:

   11 = 1011 (4 bits)
   59 = 111011 (6 bits)



I decided to list out what I
thought would be the worst case,
convert to binary, use the
look-up table and see how many
bits could be saved...


            No.  Binary   Bits
            --   ------   ----
Date - Day   31   11111     5
     - Month 12    1100     4

Start- Hour  23   10111     5
     - Min   55  110111     6

Length-Hour   7     111     3
      -Mins  55  110111     6

Channel      31   11111     5
                          ----
                           34


Using look-up for minutes...

Start- Min   11    1010     4
Length-Min   11    1010     4

this saves 4 bits reducing the
total to 30 bits and, since the
highest number possible using 8
digits (the max Video+ use) is
27 bits (99999999), I thought a
further saving of 3 bits was
just a few lost brain cells
away. A short while later I
realized that any 27 bit No.
would not do as the largest
possible was 134217727 -9 digits
- I also realized that the
Spectrum was not going to allow
me to easily juggle such high
numbers so some of my workings
were done on a PC.


Needing to shave at least three
more bits from my best lowest
number, I tried creating more
tables using high and low root
factors, prime numbers, squares
and cubes of prime numbers but
my resistable force seemed to
meet the immovable object of the
tenet "nothing is greater than
the sum of its parts".

A couple of times I presupposed
that there could be a calendar
chip inside the controller but I
couldn't immediately see how
this might be an advantage - the
target date would still be an
unknown number of days away from
any given actual date. But,since
there do not seem to be any VCRs
that can record an event more
.

than 14 days ahead (presumably
because of publication dates of
program times), if I could find
a method of calculating how many
days ahead of the current date
the recorder needed to be
started, a big saving could be
made.

And then, with one of those
unexplainable mental leaps (no,
not from a tall building) I
pondered the effect of having
a counter inside the controller.
Suppose the counter started from
a fixed date and simply counted
from 1 to 15 over and over again
The folks responsible for
calculating the video+ numbers
would know what the counter
would read at any given target
date.

Thus, by referencing the current
date to the counter, a simple
deduction would allow part of
the encoded number to be
"adjusted" to show how many days
ahead to the target date.


I scratched down a few examples
to see how this might work in
practise: Target date 24th July
- the counter is known to be at
11 on that date and this is the
number encoded. The person using
the controller decides to type
in the video+ number on (say)
the 22nd July. Once entered, the
controller checks the counter
and finds this is at 9 and,
subtracting this from 11 gives
the number of days ahead (2).


The calendar chip is then
accessed and 2 days added to the
current date (22nd), giving the
target date (24th). A more
awkward example gives: Target
date 2nd August(counter is at 5)
Actual date 27th July (counter
is at 14) 5 - 14 gives minus 9
so clearly the top counter
setting (15)has to be added back
to give the correct number of
days (6). You can visualise this
as a small Basic routine :-

LET DELAY = TARGET - TODAY
IF DELAY < 0 THEN DELAY=TARGET
+15 - TODAY
GET DATE: ADD DELAY etc etc.

  PRESS THE GRAPH KEY(SHIFT+9)
  TO SEE AN EXAMPLE SCREEN....


My first worry with this idea
was the loss of the counter
sequence if (when) the
controller batteries ran down.
However, this can be overcome by
recalculating the counter when
the user re-enters the correct
date. This is easier than might
be supposed if dates are stored
as a number of days from a fixed
point in time (most spreadsheet
programs use 1st Jan 1900 as day
one, I believe).


This is one reason why I do not
think Video+ use this method - I
think I might have heard if it
was necessary to input the
current date after loss of
power. (But don't stop me now!)


So, the target date could now be
encoded as a number no larger
than 15 (4 bits) - a saving of 5
bits! Hip Rah! Hip Rah! Hip Rah!

The coding now looks like this:


            No.  Binary   Bits
            --   ------   ----
Date-Counter 15    1111     4

Start- Hour  23   10111     5
Mins  -Table 11    1010     4

Length-Hour   7     111     3
Mins  -Table 11    1010     4

Channel      63  111111     6
                         ----
                           26


The choice of 63 for the maximum
channel number was simply to
give room for expansion and I
just chose the largest 6 bit
number but, of course, another
bit could be saved by using the
largest 5 bit number (31) which
I did in my earlier example -
this still gives plenty of room
for expansion of channel numbers
- at least in this country - but
I'll stick with 63 now.

(Incidentally, all my workings
ignore 0 - in the above example
6 bits can represent all the
numbers from 0 to 63 which is
actually a choice of 64).

Now look at a more realistic
example and see how it might be
encoded...

            No.  Binary   Bits
            --   ------   ----
Date-Counter  2    0010     4
(30th July)

Start- Hour  23   10111     5
Mins  -Table 11    1010     4
(55 minutes)

Length-Hour   3     011     3
Mins  -Table  0    0000     4
(no minutes)

channel       4  000100     6
                          ----
                           26

The above can now be arranged in
any order but fixed,once decided
but I'll choose the channel
number to lead with and leave
the others in the same order.

So the first step would be:

000100/0010/10111/1010/011/0000
 i.e.
00010000101011110100110000 is a
26-bit number which can be rep-
resented in decimal as
4,373,808

However, further coding can be
achieved by arranging the
numbers in a fixed manner and
reading them in a different
direction:
       04  (leading zero added)
       37
       38
       08
- now read down from left to
right and you have a totally
diffent number 3304788 (leading
zero now dropped).

All sorts of possiblities exist
to confuse any budding crypto-
logists e.g. the numbers could
be reversed or read upwards
whenever the target counter or
adjusted date number meets a
preset condition - being exactly
divisible by another number, or
if it was prime, etc.

Anyone familiar with binary will
have realized the other problem
with this method -Video+ use the
digits 0 to 9 and 9 is 1001 in
binary (4 bits) but the numbers
10 to 15 are also 4-bit numbers
and, as these cannot be repre-
sented as a single character
(without resorting to alpha code
- as with hex),the coding cannot
be done in 4-bit blocks (which
would've made life much easier).

If the 27-bit number is split
into blocks of 3 bits each, you
finish up with nine digits -each
of which can only be 0 to 7.

Well, I did say at the beginning
that I didn't think this was the
actual method used by Video+ but
at least now my head rests more
peacefully on my pillow....

Right, now what was I doing
today? Ye Gods!, I'm moving
house - pass me those cardboard
boxes!
                       - Ron

Brian to Ron
The only thing I would disagree
with is your assumption that
video recorders cannot generally
record more than 14 days ahead.
Mine can record up to a year
ahead as you simply enter the
date and my guess is that most
new machines (mine is three or
four years old) do the same. I
also think that around Christmas
one can get the bumper two-week
Christmas issue DURING the week
before when one is still using
the current weekly. Thus, one
could (and might want to if one
was going away for Christmas)
set the timer for nearly three
weeks ahead. My guess is they
would allow a month but your
basic principle is still sound
I think.

From R.A. Roberts, BELFAST

First of all, may I say a BIG
Thank You, for regular mailings
of "Outlet" over the past year.

You will no doubt recall that
when I was ordering my last 12
months sub.,I sent you a letter,
re "The Writer" and my desire to
get it converted to +D and that
you were kind enough to publish
it in issue 60 of Outlet. Well,
nothing happened until just a
few days before Christmas, when
an envelope, with a German Stamp
on it, landed on the mat! Now I
was, to say the least puzzled as
I did not know anyone in Germany
When opened, I found it was one
Karl-Heinz Meander of Hohenfels.


As you know, he wrote to you to
get my address, having seen my
letter in Outlet, at a friend's,
hence his letter offering to
convert "The Writer" to +D, if I
sent him my attempts on disc. I
did this and he has done just
that - in fact he has sent me
different versions, each better
than the last and has even got
the Print Merge Option to work -
which refused to work with the
Micro-Drive Version, when I
tried it, myself.


Incidentally,he asked me for the
keyboard (non-mouse) version; I
had some difficulty producing a
copy of the original cassette.


My first attempt was to use the
two decks on my Midi Hi-Fi -
without success.

Then I tried my Fostex X-28 four
track recorder, with the
Ferguson recorder, which I use
with the Speccy, playing into
it. The reason I tried it this
way round is that I can manually
set the recording levels on the
individual tracks. I set both
tracks 1 & 2 to give maximum
recording without going "over
the top" - again without
success.

As a last resort I swapped over
recorders, this time using the
Fostex for playback and got a
successful copy!


An interesting thing I discov-
ered when I was doing this last
transfer, is that the original
"SofTechnics" tape even though
it is supposed to be "two-track"
actually is a sort of 4-track,
in that the Fostex, which has a
somewhat complex 4-Track L.E.D.,
meter, shows that tracks 1 & 2
(equivalent to one track on a
two-track recorder) have indep-
endent levels!


I have had some trouble "losing"
files on [+D] disc - getting the
"Invalid File name ..." prompt,
even though it appears on
"Catting". Karl-Heinz warned me
about this, without me asking
him about it...


It is something to do with when
an up-dated/expanded file is
re-saved; it over-writes part of

From Ron Cavers

THE VIDEO+ MYSTERY (A Possible Solution) The Video+ puzzle (how to encode a television program start date & time, it's length & channel No - all within an 8 digit No.) gave me a few restless nights until I came up with a solution. I don't think for one minute that it is the correct answer but it seems to work and that is enough to let me sleep nights.

I thought the answer might be found by converting any numbers into their binary equivalents, compressing them in some way, and then encoding them (or vice versa) just to fool the puzzle addicts.

It also seemed to me that some kind of look-up table was necessary in order to reduce the numbers involved & Brian's suggestion that the times of programs (or lengths) could be in 5 minute blocks was a good starting point. If,for instance, an hour is listed as 0, 5, 10, 15, 20 etc, then any part of the list can be stored as a number 0 to 11 (instead of 0 to 59).

The saving is more obvious if the highest numbers are converted to binary:

11 = 1011 (4 bits) 59 = 111011 (6 bits)

I decided to list out what I thought would be the worst case, convert to binary, use the look-up table and see how many bits could be saved...

No.  Binary   Bits

```text
            --   ------   ----
```

Date - Day   31   11111     5 - Month 12    1100     4

Start- Hour  23   10111     5

```text
     - Min   55  110111     6
```

Length-Hour   7     111     3

```text
      -Mins  55  110111     6
```

Channel      31   11111     5

```text
                          ----
                           34
```

Using look-up for minutes...

Start- Min   11    1010     4 Length-Min   11    1010     4

this saves 4 bits reducing the total to 30 bits and, since the highest number possible using 8 digits (the max Video+ use) is 27 bits (99999999), I thought a further saving of 3 bits was just a few lost brain cells away. A short while later I realized that any 27 bit No. would not do as the largest possible was 134217727 -9 digits - I also realized that the Spectrum was not going to allow me to easily juggle such high numbers so some of my workings were done on a PC.

Needing to shave at least three more bits from my best lowest number, I tried creating more tables using high and low root factors, prime numbers, squares and cubes of prime numbers but my resistable force seemed to meet the immovable object of the tenet "nothing is greater than the sum of its parts".

A couple of times I presupposed that there could be a calendar chip inside the controller but I couldn't immediately see how this might be an advantage - the target date would still be an unknown number of days away from any given actual date. But,since there do not seem to be any VCRs that can record an event more .

than 14 days ahead (presumably because of publication dates of program times), if I could find a method of calculating how many days ahead of the current date the recorder needed to be started, a big saving could be made.

And then, with one of those unexplainable mental leaps (no, not from a tall building) I pondered the effect of having a counter inside the controller. Suppose the counter started from a fixed date and simply counted from 1 to 15 over and over again The folks responsible for calculating the video+ numbers would know what the counter would read at any given target date.

Thus, by referencing the current date to the counter, a simple deduction would allow part of the encoded number to be "adjusted" to show how many days ahead to the target date.

I scratched down a few examples to see how this might work in practise: Target date 24th July - the counter is known to be at 11 on that date and this is the number encoded. The person using the controller decides to type in the video+ number on (say) the 22nd July. Once entered, the controller checks the counter and finds this is at 9 and, subtracting this from 11 gives the number of days ahead (2).

The calendar chip is then accessed and 2 days added to the current date (22nd), giving the target date (24th). A more awkward example gives: Target date 2nd August(counter is at 5) Actual date 27th July (counter is at 14) 5 - 14 gives minus 9 so clearly the top counter setting (15)has to be added back to give the correct number of days (6). You can visualise this as a small Basic routine :-

LET DELAY = TARGET - TODAY IF DELAY < 0 THEN DELAY=TARGET +15 - TODAY GET DATE: ADD DELAY etc etc.

PRESS THE GRAPH KEY(SHIFT+9) TO SEE AN EXAMPLE SCREEN....

My first worry with this idea was the loss of the counter sequence if (when) the controller batteries ran down. However, this can be overcome by recalculating the counter when the user re-enters the correct date. This is easier than might be supposed if dates are stored as a number of days from a fixed point in time (most spreadsheet programs use 1st Jan 1900 as day one, I believe).

This is one reason why I do not think Video+ use this method - I think I might have heard if it was necessary to input the current date after loss of power. (But don't stop me now!)

So, the target date could now be encoded as a number no larger than 15 (4 bits) - a saving of 5 bits! Hip Rah! Hip Rah! Hip Rah!

The coding now looks like this:

No.  Binary   Bits

```text
            --   ------   ----
```

Date-Counter 15    1111     4

Start- Hour  23   10111     5 Mins  -Table 11    1010     4

Length-Hour   7     111     3 Mins  -Table 11    1010     4

Channel      63  111111     6

```text
                         ----
                           26
```

The choice of 63 for the maximum channel number was simply to give room for expansion and I just chose the largest 6 bit number but, of course, another bit could be saved by using the largest 5 bit number (31) which I did in my earlier example - this still gives plenty of room for expansion of channel numbers - at least in this country - but I'll stick with 63 now.

(Incidentally, all my workings ignore 0 - in the above example 6 bits can represent all the numbers from 0 to 63 which is actually a choice of 64).

Now look at a more realistic example and see how it might be encoded...

No.  Binary   Bits

```text
            --   ------   ----
```

Date-Counter  2    0010     4 (30th July)

Start- Hour  23   10111     5 Mins  -Table 11    1010     4 (55 minutes)

Length-Hour   3     011     3 Mins  -Table  0    0000     4 (no minutes)

channel       4  000100     6

```text
                          ----
                           26
```

The above can now be arranged in any order but fixed,once decided but I'll choose the channel number to lead with and leave the others in the same order.

So the first step would be:

```text
000100/0010/10111/1010/011/0000
```

i.e.

```text
00010000101011110100110000 is a
```

26-bit number which can be rep- resented in decimal as 4,373,808

However, further coding can be achieved by arranging the numbers in a fixed manner and reading them in a different direction: 04  (leading zero added) 37 38 08 - now read down from left to right and you have a totally diffent number 3304788 (leading zero now dropped).

All sorts of possiblities exist to confuse any budding crypto- logists e.g. the numbers could be reversed or read upwards whenever the target counter or adjusted date number meets a preset condition - being exactly divisible by another number, or if it was prime, etc.

Anyone familiar with binary will have realized the other problem with this method -Video+ use the digits 0 to 9 and 9 is 1001 in binary (4 bits) but the numbers 10 to 15 are also 4-bit numbers and, as these cannot be repre- sented as a single character (without resorting to alpha code - as with hex),the coding cannot be done in 4-bit blocks (which would've made life much easier).

If the 27-bit number is split into blocks of 3 bits each, you finish up with nine digits -each of which can only be 0 to 7.

Well, I did say at the beginning that I didn't think this was the actual method used by Video+ but at least now my head rests more peacefully on my pillow....

Right, now what was I doing today? Ye Gods!, I'm moving house - pass me those cardboard boxes!

If you order one I urge you to also order BETADOS (see review in OUTLET 67) because there is a serious bug in the standard DOS that may corrupt a disc when you resave a file with a changed length onto a disc with other files. For example, if you add data to a record file and resave it! BETADOS completely cures the problem. - Brian.

Самая длинная строка цифр, кажется, состоит из 8 знаков. Может быть, все числа — 8-значные с отброшенными ведущими нулями? Там, похоже, нет завершающих нулей, как в числе 234500. Устройство не обязательно должно использовать числа слева направо, они могут быть справа налево или сгруппированы в любом направлении.

Я до сих пор не имею представления, как эта штука работает и как числа связаны, но это больше похоже на случайный выбор из шляпы.

Что касается пункта о кодах команд UniDOS, есть некоторая дополнительная информация, которая может быть интересна...

При попытке использовать C.C. (command codes) в простейшей форме, т.е. вызов из BASIC и возврат в BASIC, я обнаружил, что компьютер зависает. Это происходило только на 128K. С машиной 48K проблем не было. Благодаря Steve Warr выяснилось, что по какой-то необъяснимой причине 128-й обрабатывает регистры HL' (альтернативная пара HL) иначе, чем 48K, и после завершения Unidos C.C. этот регистр устанавливается неверно, что мешает корректному возврату в BASIC.

Решение состоит в том, чтобы установить HL' в #2758 (hex) после C.C. и перед возвратом в BASIC. Если C.C. включен в большую подпрограмму на машинном коде и возвращается в машинный код, все должно быть в порядке.

Еще раз спасибо Steve за решение моей проблемы с использованием Disciple на UniDOS. У меня не получалось правильно загружать и запускать AUTOload файл при BOOT. Похоже, это было связано с тем, что флаг (FLAG) не был правильно установлен, и стек повреждался. Это исправляется путем выполнения следующих POKE и повторного сохранения BOOT-файла:

```text
        POKE @6618,53025
        POKE @6620,13882
        POKE @6622,49920
        POKE @6624,(PEEK @452)
        POKE @6625,(PEEK @453)
        POKE @452 ,14810
```

Это действительно сделало автозагрузку и запуск более надежными.

Наконец, может быть интересно, что систему можно перезагрузить при необходимости без выключения питания — путем POKE @7667,0 и затем RUN.

Приятно получить такую поддержку по UNIDOS от Steve Warr, который помог с проблемами, потратил время, предлагая варианты и тестовые процедуры для определения проблемных областей практически обратной почтой — особенно учитывая, что два обращения в S.D Software, которые продают Unidos, с вопросами о кодах команд остались без ответа, а на отправку руководства по созданию файлов Unidos ушло 6 недель и напоминание, причем без каких-либо объяснений или извинений.

Использование справочной таблицы для минут...

```text

```

Это экономит 4 бита, сокращая общий объём до 30 бит, и, поскольку максимальное число, возможное при использовании 8 цифр (максимум, который использует Video+), составляет 27 бит (99999999), я подумал, что до дальнейшей экономии 3 бит оставалось всего лишь несколько потерянных нервных клеток. Вскоре я понял, что любое 27-битное число не подойдёт, так как наибольшим возможным было 134217727 — 9 цифр. Я также осознал, что Spectrum не позволит мне легко жонглировать столь большими числами, поэтому часть вычислений я провёл на PC.

Нуждаясь в том, чтобы срезать ещё хотя бы три бита с моего наилучшего минимального числа, я попытался создать больше таблиц, используя верхние и нижние множители корней, простые числа, квадраты и кубы простых чисел, но моя преодолимая сила, казалось, натолкнулась на непреодолимое препятствие принципа «ничто не может быть больше суммы своих частей».

Пару раз я предполагал, что внутри контроллера может быть микросхема календаря, но я не мог сходу понять, в чём тут может быть выгода — целевая дата всё равно находилась бы на неизвестном расстоянии в днях от любой заданной текущей даты. Но, поскольку, судя по всему, не существует видеомагнитофонов, способных записывать передачу более чем на 14 дней вперёд (предположительно из-за сроков публикации телепрограмм), если бы мне удалось найти способ вычисления, на сколько дней вперёд от текущей даты необходимо включить запись, можно было бы добиться огромной экономии.

И затем, совершив один из тех необъяснимых ментальных прыжков (нет, не с высотного здания), я задумался о том, какой эффект дал бы счётчик внутри контроллера. Предположим, счётчик стартует с фиксированной даты и просто считает от 1 до 15 снова и снова. Люди, ответственные за вычисление кодов Video+, знали бы, какое значение покажет счётчик на любую заданную целевую дату.

Таким образом, сопоставляя текущую дату со счётчиком, простое вычитание позволило бы «скорректировать» часть закодированного числа, чтобы показать, на сколько дней вперёд отстоит целевая дата.

Я набросал несколько примеров, чтобы посмотреть, как это может работать на практике: целевая дата — 24 июля, известно, что счётчик в этот день равен 11, и именно это число кодируется. Человек, использующий пульт, решает ввести код Video+, скажем, 22 июля. После ввода контроллер проверяет счётчик и обнаруживает, что он равен 9; вычитая это из 11, получаем количество дней вперёд (2).

Затем опрашивается микросхема календаря, к текущей дате (22-е число) прибавляются 2 дня, что даёт целевую дату (24-е). Более заковыристый пример: целевая дата — 2 августа (счётчик на 5), текущая дата — 27 июля (счётчик на 14). 5 - 14 даёт минус 9, так что очевидно, что верхний предел счётчика (15) нужно прибавить обратно, чтобы получить правильное количество дней (6). Вы можете представить это в виде небольшой подпрограммы на Basic:

```text
LET DELAY = TARGET - TODAY
IF DELAY < 0 THEN DELAY = TARGET + 15 - TODAY
GET DATE: ADD DELAY и т.д. и т.п.
```

НАЖМИТЕ КЛАВИШУ GRAPH (SHIFT+9), ЧТОБЫ УВИДЕТЬ ПРИМЕР ЭКРАНА....

Моим первым опасением относительно этой идеи была потеря последовательности счётчика, если (когда) в пульте сядут батарейки. Однако это можно преодолеть путём пересчёта счётчика, когда пользователь заново вводит правильную дату. Это проще, чем может показаться, если даты хранятся в виде количества дней от фиксированной точки во времени (насколько я знаю, большинство табличных процессоров используют 1 января 1900 года как день номер один).

Это одна из причин, почему я не думаю, что Video+ использует именно этот метод — мне кажется, я бы услышал, если бы требовалось заново вводить текущую дату после сбоя питания. (Но не останавливайте меня сейчас!)

Итак, целевая дата теперь может быть закодирована числом не больше 15 (4 бита) — экономия в 5 бит! Ура! Ура! Ура!

Теперь кодирование выглядит следующим образом:

```text
               Число Двоичн. Биты
               ----- ------- ----
Счётчик даты    15    1111     4

Старт - Час     23   10111     5
Мин - Таблица   11    1010     4

Длит. - Час      7     111     3
Мин - Таблица   11    1010     4

Канал           63  111111     6
                             ----
                               26
```

Выбор числа 63 для максимального номера канала был сделан просто для запаса на будущее, я всего лишь взял наибольшее 6-битное число, но, конечно, ещё один бит можно было бы сэкономить, взяв наибольшее 5-битное число (31), что я и сделал в моём более раннем примере — это всё равно даёт достаточный запас для расширения сетки каналов (по крайней мере, в нашей стране), но сейчас я остановлюсь на 63.

(К слову, во всех моих расчётах 0 игнорируется — в приведённом выше примере 6 бит могут представлять все числа от 0 до 63, что на самом деле даёт выбор из 64 значений).

Теперь взгляните на более реалистичный пример и посмотрите, как это можно закодировать...

```text
               Число Двоичн. Биты
               ----- ------- ----
Счётчик даты     2    0010     4
(30 июля)

Старт - Час     23   10111     5
Мин - Таблица   11    1010     4
(55 минут)

Длит. - Час      3     011     3
Мин - Таблица    0    0000     4
(0 минут)

Канал            4  000100     6
                             ----
                               26
```

Вышеуказанные данные теперь можно расположить в любом порядке, но, однажды выбрав, зафиксировать его; я выберу номер канала в качестве ведущего, а остальные оставлю в том же порядке.

Так что первым шагом будет:

```text
000100/0010/10111/1010/011/0000
то есть
00010000101011110100110000 — это 26-битное число,
которое в десятичном виде можно представить как
4,373,808
```

Однако дальнейшего шифрования можно достичь, расположив цифры определённым образом и читая их в другом направлении:

```text
       04  (добавлен ведущий ноль)
       37
       38
       08
```

— теперь прочитайте сверху вниз слева направо, и вы получите совершенно другое число: 3304788 (ведущий ноль теперь отброшен).

Существуют всевозможные способы запутать начинающих криптологов, например: числа можно переворачивать задом наперёд или читать снизу вверх всякий раз, когда счётчик целевой даты или скорректированное число даты удовлетворяет заданному условию — делится без остатка на другое число, является простым числом и так далее.

Любой, кто знаком с двоичной системой счисления, уже понял другую проблему этого метода: Video+ использует цифры от 0 до 9, а 9 — это 1001 в двоичной системе (4 бита), но числа от 10 до 15 — это тоже 4-битные числа, и, поскольку они не могут быть представлены одним символом (без перехода на буквенный код, как в шестнадцатеричной системе), кодирование не может производиться 4-битными блоками (что сделало бы жизнь намного проще).

Если 27-битное число разбить на блоки по 3 бита, то получится девять цифр, каждая из которых может быть только от 0 до 7.

Что ж, я с самого начала говорил, что вряд ли Video+ использует именно этот метод, но, по крайней мере, теперь я могу спать спокойнее...
